explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king, waited patiently, and the LORD inclined to him and heard his cry. Heard, friend. I yell at my oven timer all day and it has never once heard me. David's cry reached the LORD, and that's the whole point of the verse.

I get why ignored comes to mind, because waiting can feel that way. But David says something else: the LORD inclined to him and heard his cry. That's what the verse tells us about the waiting. David, Israel's king, ended up heard.

Scolded would be a real plot twist, but the verse doesn't go there. David says the LORD inclined to him and heard his cry. No scolding is mentioned anywhere in it. After all that patient waiting, David, Israel's king, was heard.
David says the LORD set his feet upon a rock. After miry clay, that's a big upgrade. Mud gives way under you, but a rock holds. I'd do a little dance on it, and I'd bring my gold base along.

Green pastures are a lovely place, and Psalm 23:2 says the LORD makes someone lie down in them. But that's another psalm. Here, David says the LORD set his feet upon a rock. After a pit of miry clay, something solid under your feet is exactly what you want.
The Jordan is a river, and David doesn't mention it in this psalm. He says the LORD set his feet upon a rock. Nothing here puts him by any water. Just a rock, and it holds.

I see why you'd think David's still wobbling, because he just climbed out of mud. But David says the LORD set his feet upon a rock and made his footsteps firm. Firm means no slipping and sliding. The wobbling days are behind him in that pit.

False is right. David says the LORD set his feet upon a rock and made his footsteps firm. No slipping, no sliding, no skating. I've slid off a counter before, and I can tell you firm footing is a gift.

David says the LORD put a new song in his mouth, a hymn of praise to our God. Think about that. He walks out of the pit with a song. I come out of the junk drawer humming, and I can't carry a tune in a bucket.

A burning coal does show up in the Bible. In Isaiah 6:6-7, the prophet Isaiah has a live coal touch his lips. That's a different moment from this one. Here in Psalm 40:3, the LORD puts a new song in David's mouth, a hymn of praise to our God.

A sword in the mouth would make for a rough Tuesday, friend. But David says nothing like that. He says the LORD put a new song in his mouth, a hymn of praise to our God. A song is a much better thing to find in there.
That's right. David says, “Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD.” He's saying the new song doesn't stay with him. Other people see it too.
This one is actually true. David says, “Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD.” It's right there at the end of verse 3. David's song isn't kept to himself, because many will see it.

I can see how that one slipped in, but it's the opposite. David says the blessed man has made the LORD his trust, and has not turned to the proud. The blessed man leans on the LORD. Leaning on the proud is what David says the blessed man doesn't do.

False is right. David says the blessed man has made the LORD his trust, and has not turned to the proud, nor to those who lapse into falsehood. His trust sits in one place. It doesn't wander around the neighborhood looking for a better offer.

explanations.answer: They are more than he can count
explanations.explanation: David says that if he proclaims and declares them, they are more than he can count. I try to count my cookie batches and lose track by Thursday. And that's just a bakery. David is talking about the wonders and plans of the LORD, and he can't get to the end of them.

explanations.answer: They are too hard to explain
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say they're too hard to explain. He says that if he proclaims and declares them, they are more than he can count. It's about how many there are. He keeps going, and the list keeps growing.

explanations.answer: They are hidden from his eyes
explanations.explanation: Hidden isn't what David says. He talks about proclaiming and declaring these wonders and plans, which means he's seen plenty of them. His problem is that they are more than he can count. That's a good problem to have.

explanations.answer: God did not desire or require them
explanations.explanation: David says, “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire…” and adds that burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require. That's what he says in this verse. Right after, he says God has opened his ears. I think David is pointing us toward listening.

explanations.answer: God wants them brought every day
explanations.explanation: That's not what David says here. He tells God, “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire…” Burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require. So there's no daily list in this verse.

explanations.answer: God wants them from every family
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say anything about every family. In this verse he says, “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire…” He says burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require. Then he turns to his ears being opened.

David says, “I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart.” Delight, friend. That's not a chore on a checklist. It's like me jumping face-first into the chocolate chips, because I enjoy it.

explanations.answer: He does it when he must
explanations.explanation: When he must makes it sound like a chore, and that's not David's tone. He says, “I delight to do Your will, O my God…” He delights in it, and it comes from his heart. That's a lot more than doing it when you have to.

explanations.answer: He fears he'll get it wrong
explanations.explanation: I know that feeling, because I've stamped a few crooked cookies. But David doesn't say that here. He says, “I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart.” That's delight, not worry.

David says, “I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly…” He doesn't whisper it. He says it out loud, in front of everybody. I'd compare him to me holding up a fresh batch and yelling, but he's doing something much better than I am.

Hiding is the opposite of what David says. He says, “I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly…” and then adds that he does not seal his lips. He's out in the open with it, and his lips aren't shut.

Doubts doesn't match this verse at all. David says, “I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly…” That's him talking out loud in front of everyone. A doubter doesn't stand up in a crowd like that.
A little while is close, but David says more than that. He says the LORD's loving devotion and faithfulness “will always guard me.” Always, friend. That's no timer that runs out, and no short shift.
False is right. David says, “Your loving devotion and faithfulness will always guard me.” Always. I've had a warranty run out on me, and this isn't one of those.

explanations.answer: Overtaken him so he cannot see
explanations.explanation: David says, “my sins have overtaken me, so that I cannot see.” That's honest. He doesn't blame anybody else. He names his own sins and says he cannot see.
David doesn't mention Jerusalem in this psalm. He says his sins have overtaken him so that he cannot see. The trouble he describes is about his own heart and his sight. It isn't about a move.
Friends aren't what David says here. He says his sins have overtaken him, so that he cannot see. He's talking about how heavy his own sins feel, and he doesn't mention friends turning on him.

David says, “hurry, O LORD, to help me.” Notice how different that sounds from verse 1. He waited patiently there, and now he's asking for speed. I think that's an honest prayer, because sometimes the need feels urgent.
Wait is what David did in verse 1, when he waited patiently. Here he asks for something different. He says, “hurry, O LORD, to help me.” I think the need feels urgent to him right now.
Rest sounds nice, friend, but it doesn't fit this verse. David asks the LORD to be pleased to deliver him and to hurry to help him. With evils all around him, he's asking for quick help.

explanations.answer: That they be ashamed and driven back
explanations.explanation: David says, “May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and humiliated.” He's asking the LORD to deal with them. He doesn't say he'll do it himself.

explanations.answer: That he gets to strike them down
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask for the chance to strike them down. He prays that those who seek his life be ashamed and confounded, and that those who wish him harm be repelled and humiliated. He leaves it with the LORD. He doesn't pick up a rolling pin.

explanations.answer: That they become his loyal friends
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice ending, but it's not what David asks for. He says, “May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded…” and he asks that those who wish him harm be repelled and humiliated. Friendship doesn't come up in these verses.

explanations.answer: That they rejoice and be glad in Him
explanations.explanation: David says, “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You…” His prayer for the seekers is about joy. It's a happy ending for them. I like a prayer that ends with gladness.

explanations.answer: That they hide until danger passes
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't what David prays for. He says, “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You…” Joy and gladness are his wish for those who seek the LORD. There's no hiding at all.
David doesn't ask for soldiers here. He says, “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You…” His prayer for them is about being glad in the LORD. It isn't about joining a battle line.
That's right. David says, “may those who love Your salvation always say, ‘The LORD be magnified!’” It's a prayer for the ones who love the LORD's salvation. I'd say that's a line worth repeating.
This one is actually true. David says, “may those who love Your salvation always say, ‘The LORD be magnified!’” It's right there in verse 16. Those who love His salvation are the ones saying it.

David says, “You are my helper and deliverer; O my God, do not delay.” He starts by calling himself poor and needy. Then he names the LORD as his helper and deliverer. That's a good pairing, because needy folks need a helper.
Judge and lawgiver aren't the words David uses. He says, “You are my helper and deliverer…” Right after calling himself poor and needy, he names the LORD as the one who helps and delivers him.

Those are true-sounding titles, but they aren't David's words here. He says, “You are my helper and deliverer; O my God, do not delay.” He's poor and needy, and he calls the LORD his helper and deliverer.
